result.summary: Pausanias describes how Dorians took Phlius after the return of the Heraclidæ, and how the exile Hippasus was an ancestor of Pythagoras. He then tours the temples, statues and sights of Phlius and closes with the tale of Hercules killing the cupbearer Cyathus.

scenes.title: Dorians take Phlius
scenes.summary: After the Heraclidæ return, Rhegnidas marches on Phlius. The citizens split, and Hippasus's party flees to Samos; his descendant was Pythagoras.
scenes.stakes: The Phliasians risk losing their land and independence to Dorian conquerors.

scenes.title: Sights of Phlius
scenes.summary: Pausanias describes the citadel grove and temple of Hebe, other sanctuaries, the bronze goat, the seer's house and the temples of Dionysus, Apollo and Isis.

scenes.title: Hercules kills Cyathus
scenes.summary: Hercules, displeased with the drink, strikes the cupbearer Cyathus dead while Œneus visits. The Phliasians built a chapel to him.
scenes.stakes: Cyathus is killed by a single blow.

alias_notes.explanation: Older Phliasians called the goddess Ganymeda; later ones called her Hebe.

notable_quotes.reason: Phlius claims to hold the Omphalus, the supposed centre of the Peloponnese.

analysis.text: Local tradition and cult shape the town's identity, from the Dorian conquest to the honours paid to gods and heroes.
The passage reflects the Dorian settlement after the legendary return of the Heraclidæ and shows sanctuary rights for slaves at Hebe's shrine.

legacy.text: Pythagoras, linked here to Phlian exiles, became the famous philosopher and mathematician.

fun_facts.text: Pausanias notes the Satyr-drama carvings of Pratinas and Aristias ranked just after Æschylus.

language_notes.text: The Heraclidæ, descendants of Hercules, returned to the Peloponnese and, with Dorian allies, conquered much of it; Arcadia alone was spared.
"Hoary from old antiquity" means whitened or venerable with great age; the temple looks extremely ancient.
Homer's references are to the Iliad (Hebe as cupbearer) and the Odyssey (Hebe as wife of Hercules in the underworld scene). Hebe is goddess of youth.
"Entire immunity" means suppliant slaves could not be punished or seized; the sanctuary gave them asylum.
The "sacred reason" is a religious explanation Pausanias leaves unstated; he only notes the nearby Hera temple.
Omphalus means "navel"; such stones marked a claimed centre of a region. Pausanias doubts the Phliasian claim.
Hercules' eleventh labour was fetching the golden apples of the Hesperides from the far west.
"Struck on the head with one of his fingers" means a mere flick of a finger, showing Hercules' enormous strength.

context_notes.text: Pythagoras, the famous philosopher and mathematician, was said to have been born on Samos.
Æsculapius was the god of healing; his statues are often bearded, so a beardless one is notable.
The She-Goat is the star Capella, whose rising was believed to bring storms and harm to vines.
Pratinas was a tragic poet from Phlius, credited with developing satyr plays; Aristias was his son.
Amphiaraus was a famous seer of Argos who died in the war of the Seven against Thebes; his oracle involved sleeping to receive dreams.

literary_notes.text: Honouring the goat statue to appease the star is a mild irony: a bronze image is treated as able to avert real harm.
Pausanias hedges between competing local versions, showing his habit of reporting traditions without vouching for them.
The casual lethal blow portrays Hercules as immensely strong and short-tempered, a hero whose power is hard to control.
